paragraphs.paraphrase: While Odysseus stays behind praying, the girl (Nausicaa, the king's daughter, as the end of the paragraph implies) drives the mule wagon home, where her handsome brothers unhitch the mules and carry the clothes indoors. She goes to her room, where her old servant and former nurse Eurymedusa lights a fire and brings her supper. Eurymedusa had been brought by ship from Apeira and picked out as a prize for King Alcinous, because he was king and his people revered him like a god.

barriers.quote: So Odysseus waited and prayed
barriers.my_reading: He has stayed behind somewhere outside the town after meeting the girl, and is praying to an unnamed god; where he is and why he is waiting is not said in this Book.
barriers.note: depends on the previous Book

barriers.quote: the girl
barriers.my_reading: Nausicaa, King Alcinous's daughter. She is only named at the end of the paragraph, and only indirectly, as the person Eurymedusa nursed.

barriers.quote: carried the clothes into the house
barriers.my_reading: A load of clothes she had taken out in the wagon, probably laundry; this Book never says what they are.
barriers.note: outside knowledge only (the washing trip in the previous Book)

barriers.quote: had been chosen as a prize for Alcinous
barriers.my_reading: She was a captive carried off from Apeira, and as king Alcinous was given her as his special share of the spoils, i.e. she was enslaved. The text never says captive or slave, and 'prize' can read as an award or a reward; the 'because he was king' logic only makes sense once you see it as a share of plunder.

paragraphs.paraphrase: After a while Odysseus sets off for the town, and the goddess Athena wraps him in a thick mist so that none of the haughty Phaeacians will insult or question him. As he enters the town, Athena comes to meet him disguised as a little girl carrying a water jug and stands in front of him, and he speaks to her.

barriers.quote: Presently
barriers.my_reading: Soon, after a while (not 'at present').
barriers.note: recurs in ¶13 and ¶22; many readers now use 'presently' to mean 'currently'

paragraphs.paraphrase: Odysseus politely asks the 'girl' to show him King Alcinous's house, explaining that he is a foreigner in trouble who knows nobody in the town or the country.

Athena, still disguised, agrees, saying Alcinous lives near her own father; she will walk ahead, but he must not speak, look at anyone or ask questions, because the people here dislike strangers. The Phaeacians are seafarers whose ships, by the favor of the sea god Poseidon, move as fast as thought or a bird in flight.

barriers.quote: father stranger
barriers.my_reading: A polite way for a child to address an older man she does not know, roughly 'sir' or 'old stranger'; not a claim that he is her father.
barriers.note: sounds odd aloud, especially next to 'my own father' in the same speech; recurs in ¶5

paragraphs.paraphrase: Athena leads and Odysseus follows through the middle of the city, unseen by anyone because she has hidden him in a thick cloud of darkness. He admires the harbors, ships, meeting places and the high city walls with a fence of stakes along the top, and at the palace Athena speaks again.

barriers.quote: palisade
barriers.my_reading: A fence of pointed wooden stakes running along the top of the walls.

barriers.quote: a thick cloud of darkness
barriers.my_reading: The same magic mist as in ¶1, making him invisible, not literal night; hard to picture him admiring the city while wrapped in 'darkness'.
barriers.note: mist / cloud of darkness / cloak of darkness / miraculous darkness all seem to name one thing

paragraphs.paraphrase: At the palace Athena tells him that important people will be at dinner inside, but he should walk straight in without fear, since boldness wins even for a stranger, and go first to the queen, Arete, who belongs to the same family as her husband Alcinous. Both are descended from Poseidon, who fathered Nausithous with the beautiful Periboea, youngest daughter of Eurymedon, a former king of the giants who destroyed his own people and died himself.

barriers.quote: carry his point
barriers.my_reading: Get what he asks for; succeed.
barriers.note: old-fashioned idiom

barriers.quote: she comes of the same family as her husband Alcinous
barriers.my_reading: She is a blood relative of her husband; ¶6 shows she is his brother's daughter, i.e. his niece, though the text never says so outright.

barriers.quote: who was father to Nausithous by Periboea
barriers.my_reading: Poseidon was Nausithous's father and Periboea his mother.
barriers.note: 'by' for the mother is old-fashioned; the chain Poseidon, Nausithous, Periboea, Eurymedon, then Rhexenor, Alcinous, Arete is hard to hold in the head, especially read aloud

barriers.quote: reigned over the giants, but he ruined his ill-fated people
barriers.my_reading: Eurymedon was king of a race of giants and somehow brought them to destruction; who the giants were and what he did is not explained.
barriers.note: outside knowledge only; not needed for the story

paragraphs.paraphrase: Athena continues: Poseidon slept with Eurymedon's daughter Periboea, and she bore him Nausithous, who became king of the Phaeacians and had two sons, Rhexenor and Alcinous. The god Apollo killed Rhexenor when he was newly married and had no son, but he left a daughter, Arete, whom Alcinous (her uncle) married and honors more than any other wife in the world is honored.

barriers.quote: Poseidon, however, lay with his daughter
barriers.my_reading: 'his' = Eurymedon's, so the daughter is Periboea from the previous paragraph, and 'lay with' = slept with. On first pass 'his' reads as Poseidon's own daughter; the sentence also repeats what ¶5 already said, so it can sound like a second event.
barriers.note: first-pass misread; 'however' has no clear contrast

barriers.quote: while he was still a bridegroom and without a son
barriers.my_reading: Rhexenor was newly married and had no male heir when Apollo killed him; why Apollo killed him is not said, and 'still a bridegroom' sits oddly with his leaving a daughter.
barriers.note: why 'without a son' matters (the throne passing to Alcinous) is left implicit

barriers.quote: whom Alcinous married, and honors more than any other woman who keeps house beside her husband
barriers.my_reading: Alcinous married his brother's daughter, his niece, and honors her more than any other wife anywhere is honored by her husband.
barriers.note: the dangling 'and honors' is awkward; the uncle-niece marriage must be worked out by the reader

paragraphs.paraphrase: Arete has always been deeply respected by her children, her husband and the whole people, who treat her like a goddess and greet her in the streets. She is wise and kind-hearted and even helps settle disputes, including men's, for the families of women she is friendly with. If Odysseus wins her goodwill, Athena says, he can hope to see his own people again and get home safely.

barriers.quote: when any women are friends of hers she will help their husbands also to settle their disputes
barriers.my_reading: She acts as a respected judge who settles quarrels, even men's, for the families of women she favors. Whose disputes these are (between the men? between husbands and wives?) and why it matters to Odysseus is unclear.

barriers.quote: seeing your friends again
barriers.my_reading: Seeing his own people, family and loved ones again; a modern reader takes 'friends' literally.
barriers.note: outside knowledge only (older usage of 'friends' = kin and dear ones); small consequence, but this Book never mentions his family otherwise; recurs in ¶12

paragraphs.paraphrase: Athena leaves Scheria (evidently the Phaeacians' land) and crosses the sea to Marathon and Athens, entering the house of someone called Erechtheus. Odysseus goes to Alcinous's palace and stops, thinking hard, before its bronze threshold, dazzled because the building shines like the sun or moon. Its walls are bronze from end to end with a blue enamel band along the top; the doors are gold, hung on silver doorposts rising from a bronze floor, with a silver beam over the door and a gold door handle.

barriers.quote: Scheria
barriers.my_reading: The name of the Phaeacians' land or island where the story is set; the text never says so directly.

barriers.quote: the home of Erechtheus
barriers.my_reading: Some place in Athens connected with Athena; no idea from the text who Erechtheus is or why she goes there.
barriers.note: outside knowledge only

barriers.quote: cornice
barriers.my_reading: A decorative band or ledge running along the top of the walls.

barriers.quote: lintel
barriers.my_reading: The horizontal beam across the top of the doorway.

barriers.quote: the hook of the door
barriers.my_reading: The door handle or latch, or a ring you pull the door by.

paragraphs.paraphrase: On each side of the door stand gold and silver guard dogs made by Hephaestus to watch over the palace, and being his work they are immortal and never age; inside, benches with fine woven covers made by the palace women line the walls, where the Phaeacian leaders feast all year, lit at night by golden statues of youths holding torches. Fifty maids work in the house grinding grain, weaving and spinning, their shuttles flickering like aspen leaves and their linen so tightly woven that oil runs off it. The Phaeacian women are the best weavers in the world, as the men are the best sailors, because Athena taught them her crafts.

barriers.quote: so they were immortal and could never grow old
barriers.my_reading: The metal guard dogs (mastiffs) are magical, ageless guardians because a divine craftsman made them; unclear whether they are statues or somehow alive.
barriers.note: Hephaestus is not introduced; that he is a god is outside knowledge only

barriers.quote: here and there from one end to the other
barriers.my_reading: 'here and there' seems to mean 'on both sides', i.e. benches ran along the walls on either side all the way, not 'scattered'.

barriers.quote: There are fifty maidservants in the house
barriers.my_reading: The narration switches from past to present tense for the household and garden, returning to the past in the last sentence of ¶10.

barriers.quote: their shuttles go backward and forward like the fluttering of aspen leaves
barriers.my_reading: The weaving tools dart back and forth across the looms as fast and constantly as aspen leaves trembling in a breeze.
barriers.note: needs knowing what a shuttle is and how aspen leaves move

barriers.quote: the linen is so closely woven that it sheds oil
barriers.my_reading: The cloth is so tight that oil runs off it instead of soaking in; why oil would be on linen at all is unclear.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Outside the gate of the outer courtyard is a walled orchard of about four acres, full of pears, pomegranates, apples, figs and olives that bear fruit all year, because the mild air ripens a new crop before the old one falls. The vineyard likewise has grapes at every stage at once (drying into raisins, being picked, being trodden for wine, just forming, changing color), and at the far end there are flower beds that bloom all year. Two streams run through: one is channeled around the garden, the other runs under the outer courtyard to the house, where the townspeople draw water; these were the gods' gifts to Alcinous's palace.

barriers.quote: Pear grows on pear, apple on apple, and fig on fig
barriers.my_reading: As each fruit ripens another follows, so there is always fruit; not fruit literally growing out of fruit.

barriers.quote: the one turned in ducts throughout the whole garden
barriers.my_reading: One stream is led through irrigation channels all around the garden.
barriers.note: 'ducts' suggests modern pipes or air ducts

paragraphs.paraphrase: After looking his fill, Odysseus crosses the threshold into the courtyard, where the Phaeacian leaders are making their customary last drink offerings to the god Hermes before going home for the night. Still invisible, he walks straight through to Arete and Alcinous and puts his hands on the queen's knees, and at that moment the magic darkness vanishes. Everyone is struck silent to see a man suddenly there, and he immediately begins his plea.

barriers.quote: making their drink offerings to Hermes
barriers.my_reading: A bedtime ritual in which they pour out some wine in honor of the god Hermes. The text never says what a drink offering physically involves (poured away? drunk as a toast?) or why Hermes.
barriers.note: drink offerings recur in ¶14, ¶15, ¶16 and ¶19

barriers.quote: laid his hands on the knees of the queen
barriers.my_reading: A formal gesture of begging for help and protection (the 'suppliant' of ¶14), not an act of familiarity.
barriers.note: the custom is never explained and can read as oddly intimate

paragraphs.paraphrase: Odysseus addresses Queen Arete as the daughter of Rhexenor and humbly begs her, her husband and their guests to help him get home to his own country quickly. He wishes the guests long and happy lives and that they may pass their wealth and public honors on to their children, since he has suffered a long time far from his own people.

barriers.quote: and all the honors the state has conferred on them
barriers.my_reading: Part of a blessing: may they also hand down to their children the honors and privileges their people have given them.
barriers.note: long chain of 'may ... and may ... and all' clauses, plus a switch from 'you' to 'them', is hard to follow aloud

paragraphs.paraphrase: He then sits down among the ashes of the hearth, and everyone stays silent until the old nobleman Echeneus, a fine speaker and one of the Phaeacian elders, speaks frankly to them.

barriers.quote: sat down on the hearth among the ashes
barriers.my_reading: He deliberately sits in the ashes by the fire as a sign of humility, like a beggar asking for protection; the meaning of the gesture is only hinted at in ¶14.

barriers.quote: the old hero Echeneus
barriers.my_reading: 'hero' here seems to mean a nobleman or chief, not someone who has done something brave.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Echeneus tells Alcinous that it does him no credit to leave a stranger sitting in the ashes of his hearth while everyone waits for the king to act. He should seat the man on a silver-inlaid chair, have wine and water mixed for an offering to Zeus the thunder god, who protects well-meaning people who come begging for help, and have the housekeeper give him supper from whatever food there is.

barriers.quote: it is not creditable to you
barriers.my_reading: It does not do you credit; it reflects badly on you.
barriers.note: easy to confuse with 'not credible' on a quick read

barriers.quote: well-disposed suppliants
barriers.my_reading: People who come in good faith to beg for help and protection; Zeus protects them, which is why the stranger must be treated well.
barriers.note: 'suppliant' is unfamiliar to many readers and is the key to the knee-clasping and the ashes

paragraphs.paraphrase: Alcinous takes Odysseus by the hand, raises him from the hearth and seats him in the chair of his favorite son Laodamas, who had been sitting next to him. A maid pours water from a golden jug over his hands into a silver basin and sets a table beside him, and a senior servant serves him bread and plenty of other food, which he eats. Alcinous then tells the servant Pontonous to mix wine and pass it round for offerings to Zeus, protector of suppliants.

barriers.quote: golden ewer
barriers.my_reading: A large golden jug for pouring water.

barriers.quote: An upper servant
barriers.my_reading: A senior household servant, probably the housekeeper Echeneus mentioned.
barriers.note: old-fashioned term

paragraphs.paraphrase: Pontonous mixes the wine and water and serves everyone, apparently first putting a little in each man's cup for the ritual offering. When they have made their offerings and drunk as much as they want, Alcinous speaks.

barriers.quote: handed it round after giving every man his drink offering
barriers.my_reading: He seems to pour a first splash into each man's cup so each can offer it to the god, then serve them wine to drink; the order of events and what 'giving' an offering means are hard to picture.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Alcinous tells the Phaeacian leaders to go home to bed, saying that tomorrow he will invite more elders to a sacrificial feast in the guest's honor and they will plan how to send him home quickly, comfortably and safely by ship, however far away it is, after which he must take whatever fate he was born to, like anyone. He adds that the stranger might be a god in disguise, but that would be unusual, since the gods normally show themselves openly to the Phaeacians at their sacrifices and feasts and do not hide even from a lone traveler. The reason he gives is that the Phaeacians are as closely related to the gods as the Cyclopes and the wild giants are.

barriers.quote: Aldermen and town councilors
barriers.my_reading: The Phaeacian nobles and elders who advise the king.
barriers.note: modern local-government terms; 'aldermen' is unfamiliar to many and feels out of place in this setting

barriers.quote: the question of his escort
barriers.my_reading: Arranging a ship and crew to take him home, not a bodyguard or companion.
barriers.note: recurs in ¶19 and ¶25

barriers.quote: they have made themselves perfectly clear to us
barriers.my_reading: The gods have always appeared openly, in visible form; not the modern idiom 'explained themselves clearly'.

barriers.quote: But in that case the gods are departing from their usual practice
barriers.my_reading: If he is a god it would be strange, because gods normally come to the Phaeacians undisguised, while this man arrived hidden; the link to his invisible arrival is left for the reader to make.

barriers.quote: as near of kin to the gods as the Cyclopes and the savage giants are
barriers.my_reading: The Phaeacians claim to be close relatives of the gods, like two other god-descended races; who the Cyclopes are, and why comparing themselves with 'savage' peoples counts as a boast, is unclear.
barriers.note: Cyclopes known from outside knowledge only

paragraphs.paraphrase: Odysseus tells Alcinous not to think he is a god: he is wholly mortal and as wretched as the most afflicted people they know, and his full story of god-sent suffering would make him seem even worse off. Still, he asks to be allowed to eat despite his grief, because hunger demands attention and makes a man forget his sorrows. He asks them to start arranging his journey at dawn, saying he would die content once he had seen his property, his servants and his great house again.

barriers.quote: let me have my supper in spite of sorrow
barriers.my_reading: 'Let me go on eating despite my grief'; but he was already served and ate in ¶15, so it reads oddly as a fresh request.

barriers.quote: my bondservants
barriers.my_reading: His slaves or servants bound to him.
barriers.note: archaic

paragraphs.paraphrase: Everyone approves his sensible words and agrees that he should be sent home; after a last drink offering they all go home to bed, leaving Odysseus with Arete and Alcinous while servants clear away the meal. Arete speaks first, because she recognizes the shirt, cloak and clothes he is wearing as made by her and her maids. She asks who he is, where he comes from, who gave him those clothes, and whether he didn't say he had come from overseas.

barriers.quote: in the gallery
barriers.my_reading: Some part of the hall, perhaps a covered colonnade, where they had been dining; hard to picture, since the scene was set in a courtyard by a hearth.

barriers.quote: Did you not say you had come here from beyond the sea?
barriers.my_reading: She is hinting at a contradiction: if he came from overseas, how is he wearing clothes made in her own house? She is probing, not just asking.
barriers.note: he has not actually said 'from beyond the sea' in this Book

paragraphs.paraphrase: Odysseus says his whole story would take too long, as the gods have treated him harshly, but answers her: far away is the island of Ogygia, where the cunning, powerful goddess Calypso, daughter of Atlas, lives alone. He came there alone after Zeus smashed his ship with thunderbolts in mid-ocean and all his comrades drowned; he clung to the keel and drifted for nine days until the gods brought him to her island on the tenth night. Calypso took him in and treated him very kindly, and even wanted to make him immortal and ageless, but he would not agree.

barriers.quote: called ‘the Ogygian.’
barriers.my_reading: The island's name is Ogygia, 'the Ogygian island'; giving an adjective as the name is odd.

barriers.quote: I stuck to the keel
barriers.my_reading: He clung to the long bottom beam of the wrecked ship and floated on it.

paragraphs.paraphrase: He stayed seven years with Calypso, weeping all the time onto the fine clothes she gave him, until in the eighth year she told him to go, whether because Zeus ordered it or because she changed her mind, and sent him off on a raft stocked with bread and wine, with sturdy clothes and a warm favorable wind. After seventeen days he sighted the mountains of the Phaeacians' coast on the eighteenth, but Poseidon stopped him with a great storm. The raft broke up in the huge seas and he had to swim until wind and current carried him to their shore.

barriers.quote: of her own free will, either because Zeus had told her she must
barriers.my_reading: She let him go without his having to escape or beg, though whether it was really her choice or Zeus's order he does not know; 'of her own free will' seems to contradict 'Zeus had told her she must'.

barriers.quote: Poseidon would let me go no further
barriers.my_reading: The sea god Poseidon is hostile to Odysseus, but this Book never says why, which is puzzling since ¶3 and ¶5 present him as the Phaeacians' patron and ancestor.
barriers.note: motive is outside knowledge only / from earlier Books

paragraphs.paraphrase: He could not land at first because the waves dashed him on the rocks, so he swam on to a sheltered, rock-free river mouth, climbed out, and at nightfall covered himself with leaves in a thicket and slept deeply through the night and the next day. Waking in the late afternoon, he saw the king's daughter playing on the beach with her maids, looking like a goddess, and begged her for help; she was more sensible than her age would suggest, gave him bread and wine, had him washed in the river and gave him the clothes he is wearing. That, he says, painful as it was to tell, is the whole truth.

barriers.quote: Sick and sorry as I was
barriers.my_reading: Ill and miserable ('sorry' = wretched, not apologetic).

barriers.quote: I have told you the whole truth
barriers.my_reading: He has explained the clothes and his route here, but he still has not said who he is or where his home is, although Arete asked; 'the whole truth' can make a reader think his identity is now known to them.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Alcinous says his daughter was wrong not to bring the stranger straight to the palace with her maids, since she was the first person he asked for help.

Odysseus asks him not to scold her: she did tell him to follow along with the maids, but he held back out of embarrassment and fear that the king might be displeased to see him, since everyone is sometimes suspicious and quick to take offense.

barriers.quote: I thought you might perhaps be displeased if you saw me
barriers.my_reading: He feared the king would be suspicious at seeing a strange man arrive with his young daughter; the reason is only hinted at.
barriers.note: outside knowledge only: in the previous Book it was the girl who asked him to wait behind, so he is tactfully taking the blame; nothing in this Book signals that

paragraphs.paraphrase: Alcinous says he is not one to get angry without cause, and, swearing by Zeus, Athena and Apollo, says that since the stranger is so like-minded he wishes he would stay, marry his daughter and become his son-in-law, and would give him a house and estate. But nobody will keep him against his will: tomorrow Alcinous will arrange the voyage, and he can sleep the whole way while the crew take him over calm seas home or anywhere else, even beyond Euboea. Phaeacian sailors who once carried Rhadamanthus to see Tityus reported Euboea as the farthest place of all, yet they did the round trip in one day with ease, which proves how superior his ships and rowers are.

barriers.quote: even if it is a long way further off than Euboea
barriers.my_reading: Euboea must be a place the Phaeacians think of as extremely far away.
barriers.note: Euboea is not explained; outside knowledge only

barriers.quote: When my people took yellow-haired Rhadamanthus to see Tityus the son of Gaia
barriers.my_reading: A past voyage in which Phaeacian sailors carried someone called Rhadamanthus to visit someone called Tityus; who they are and why is unknown, and only the point (a very long voyage done in a day) comes through.
barriers.note: outside knowledge only

barriers.quote: those of them who saw it told me it is the furthest place of any
barriers.my_reading: 'it' seems to be Euboea, the destination of that voyage, rather than Tityus or the voyage itself.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Delighted, Odysseus prays aloud to Zeus that Alcinous will do everything he has promised, which will win the king undying fame and bring Odysseus home.

When they have finished talking, Arete has her maids make up a bed for Odysseus in a room in the gatehouse, with good red rugs, covers on top and woolen cloaks for him to wrap up in. The maids go out with torches, make the bed and come to tell him it is ready, and he gladly goes to rest.

barriers.quote: good red rugs
barriers.my_reading: Thick colored blankets or throws laid on the bed, not floor rugs.

barriers.quote: woolen cloaks for Odysseus to wear
barriers.my_reading: Woolen cloaks to wrap himself in as blankets while he sleeps.

paragraphs.paraphrase: Odysseus sleeps in the room over the echoing entrance gateway, while Alcinous sleeps in the inner part of the palace with the queen beside him.

barriers.quote: a room over the echoing gateway
barriers.my_reading: A room at the palace entrance, away from the family's inner rooms; 'over' the gateway does not quite match 'in the gatehouse' (¶27), and why it is 'echoing' is unclear.

book_level: Drink offerings run through the whole evening (¶11, ¶14-¶16, ¶19) but are never explained: what physically happens (poured out for the god? drunk?) is unclear, and ¶16's 'giving every man his drink offering' is especially hard to picture. Mixing wine with water is also unexplained.

The suppliant ritual carries the key scene but is never explained: clasping the queen's knees, sitting in the hearth ashes, 'well-disposed suppliants'. Readers can infer begging, but not why these gestures oblige the hosts.

Athena's family-tree speech (¶5-¶7) is dense and hard to follow, especially aloud: 'Poseidon, however, lay with his daughter' first reads as Poseidon's own daughter, and the reader has to work out that Alcinous married his own niece.

Old-fashioned words and idioms keep slowing the reading: 'presently' (= soon), 'father stranger', 'carry his point', 'not creditable', 'sick and sorry', 'bondservants', 'upper servant', 'aldermen and town councilors', and 'escort' meaning passage home by ship.

'Friends' (¶7, ¶12) seems to mean family or his own people. Together with ¶18's wish to see his 'property ... bondservants ... house', the Book never shows that Odysseus longs for his family, so his motives read as more material than they are probably meant to be.

The palace description (¶8-¶10) piles up unfamiliar building and craft terms (cornice, lintel, hook of the door, palisade, mastiffs, shuttles, oil-shedding linen, ducts) and slips into the present tense. The layout of courtyard, hearth, 'gallery', gatehouse and 'room over the echoing gateway' is hard to picture.

Mythological names are dropped without explanation (Erechtheus, the giants, Cyclopes, Rhadamanthus, Tityus, Gaia, Euboea, Hephaestus, Atlas). The point of each passage mostly survives, but any sense of who these figures are comes from outside knowledge only.

The reader is left to work out several story points: why Poseidon, the Phaeacians' ancestor and patron, is hostile to Odysseus; that Odysseus still never gives his name despite Arete's direct question (while claiming 'the whole truth'); and that his account of the princess in ¶24 is a tactful cover for her, which is clear only from the previous Book (outside knowledge only).
